issues.legal_issue: Co-landlords including both an expedited-procedure-eligible landlord and landlords outside that class may jointly choose the forum for a tenant eviction claim based on a requirement common to them.
material_facts: The premises were jointly owned by a widow and her two major sons, who succeeded to ownership after the former owner’s death.
The widow belonged to a category eligible to use the special eviction procedure, while her sons did not.
All three co-landlords joined in eviction proceedings before the Rent Controlling Authority, relying on a requirement for the sons’ businesses.
The sons did not object to the widow maintaining the proceedings, and the pleaded requirement was one that could support a claim by the widow as well as by the sons.
issues.conclusion: The co-landlords could choose to proceed before the Rent Controlling Authority or bring a civil suit; the proceedings before the Authority were competent and maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 23-A(b) and 23-J, a landlord in a specified eligible category may seek eviction through the special procedure for a qualifying non-residential business requirement, including the business of a major son. Sections 12(1)(f), 11-A and 45 govern the civil-court route and the Authority’s jurisdiction. A co-owner may sue for eviction without joining all other co-owners if they do not object (Sri Ram Pasricha v. Jagannath; Kanta Goel v. B.P. Pathan; Pal Singh v. Sunder Singh). The special procedure remains available when eligible and non-eligible co-landlords jointly advance a common claim; the presence of the non-eligible co-landlords does not alter its character (Shivraj Jat v. Smt. Asha Lata Yadav; Harbans Singh v. Smt. Margrat G. Bhingardive). The choice also accords with the principles that a plaintiff controls the action and that a right should have a remedy and a forum (Smt. Ganga Bai v. Vijay Kumar).

rule.if: tenant_eviction_proceeding and co_landlords_jointly_claiming and special_class_landlord_present and common_requirement_supports_claim_of_all

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord or landlords initiated proceedings seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.co_landlords_jointly_claiming: Two or more co-landlords joined in advancing the eviction claim.
predicates.special_class_landlord_present: At least one of the joined co-landlords belonged to a class eligible to use a special, expedited eviction procedure.
predicates.common_requirement_supports_claim_of_all: The requirement pleaded could support an eviction claim by the eligible landlord and by the other joined co-landlords.

issues.definition: When co-landlords jointly bring a tenant eviction claim based on a requirement common to them and at least one is eligible for the special procedure, they may choose either competent forum.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord establishes a bona fide requirement for non-residential business use when the business need is supported by evidence and there is no other owned accommodation that is reasonably suitable for that use.
material_facts: The shops were let for non-residential purposes.
The landlords sought one shop for a major son to start a business and the other for a major son to continue his business.
The Rent Controlling Authority and the High Court found the claimed requirements proved after evaluating the evidence.
The landlords had no other owned accommodation suitable for the claimed needs.
Other premises identified by the tenants were rented, or were on an upper floor and not reasonably suitable as substitutes for ground-floor shops.
issues.conclusion: The landlords proved bona fide requirements for the shops, and the alternative premises identified by the tenants did not defeat those requirements.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 23-A(b) and 12(1)(f) require a bona fide non-residential business need and the absence of other reasonably suitable accommodation of the landlord’s own. An alternative must be reasonably suitable in comparison with the premises sought; a rented premises is not an alternative accommodation of the landlord’s own. Once the need is found bona fide, the landlord’s choice among available accommodations is respected unless an equally suitable and convenient alternative is unreasonably refused (Shiv Sarup Gupta v. Dr. Mahesh Chand Gupta). A landlord cannot be compelled to conduct a business from rented premises.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_proceeding and nonresidential_business_requirement and business_need_supported_by_evidence and no_owned_reasonably_suitable_alternative and identified_alternatives_are_rented_or_unsuitable

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant from premises let for non-residential use.
predicates.nonresidential_business_requirement: The landlord sought the premises to start or continue a business, including a major child’s business.
predicates.business_need_supported_by_evidence: The evidence supported the claimed need to use the premises for the stated business purpose.
predicates.no_owned_reasonably_suitable_alternative: The landlord had no other owned accommodation in the relevant area reasonably suitable for the business use.
predicates.identified_alternatives_are_rented_or_un: Premises identified as alternatives were rented by the landlord or were not reasonably suitable substitutes for the premises sought.

issues.definition: When an eviction claim concerns non-residential business use, evidence supports the business need, no suitable owned alternative exists, and identified alternatives are rented or unsuitable, the requirement is established as bona fide.
